== History ==
Before Savage wrote The Compleat Angler, he had written a poem on a similar theme, "One night two men from Egulac", which he entered in the poetry competition at the Royal Society of Literature in 1675.  The poem was commended, but it did not win the prize.  Later, in 1676, the poem was published as a broadside and included in the book The Compleat Angler.  The poem is about two native American fishermen who catch a sturgeon and argue about who should have the honour of scaling and cleaning the fish.  The argument grows so heated that one of the men draws a knife and threatens to use it.  The other man, who is called Tecumseh, calms down his companion and prevents a fight.  The poem is significant as one of the earliest works of literature in the American literary tradition and as a work that reflects the tensions that could arise between native Americans and European settlers.

Context
This is a line from a poem by Algernon Charles Swinburne titled "The Two Men of Egulac." It is the first line of the first stanza.

Explanation
Egulac is a place mentioned in other works by Swinburne, and is generally held to be a reference to Egra, a town in the Sinai Peninsula. The poem as a whole is a work of art, and like much of Swinburne's poetry, it defies simple explanation. It is, however, generally agreed upon by scholars that the poem is about two men from Egra who go to a nearby village.

Full text
The two men of Egulac,
One night, two men from Egulac,
Went to a nearby village
To see what the villagers could see.
There was much talk of a strange sight
That had been seen in the village that night.
One night two men from Egulac
Came to the place where the sight had been.
There were the prints of a giant's feet
And the villagers said that it was he
Who had come to visit the village that night.
One night two men from Egulac
Went to the place where the giant's prints were.
There they saw a sight that amazed them
A giant, yes, but much more than that,
For in one hand he bore a torch,
In the other, a book of old.

And asked for a light, and I took them in;
They spoke me fair, and I began to think
That they were not robbers, as their looks might seem;
So I rose from the table, and I filled their cup,
And we three sat down to drink a pleasanter brew;
They told me of a place where all was right,
And where such as ourselves might live, and might
Have goodly possessions, and be rich and rare;
But, alas! we were undone, because we were poor,
And had not the money to buy a single share;
They said, "We will not rob you, nor put you to shame,
But we will go away, and leave you to your fame."

This can take place within minutes or up to an hour after the person has been rescued. The symptoms are the same as those for primary drowning: difficulty breathing, exhaustion, and eventually loss of consciousness. The key difference is that with secondary drowning, the person has usually been out of the water for some time before these symptoms appear.

The story also illustrates the theme of transformation, as the natives in the story are able to transform their canoe into a house and then back again.

This can take place within minutes or up to an hour after the person has been saved. The symptoms are the same as those for primary drowning: difficulty breathing, exhaustion, and eventually loss of consciousness.
